title: Council Post: The Transformative Impact Of AI On Financial Services
text:
Gianluca Sidoti is an Independent Financial Advisor, Founder of TraDetector and Managing Partner at Citadines Capital SCF.
In the rapidly evolving world of finance, artificial intelligence (AI) stands out as a transformative force reshaping the landscape of financial services. As an independent financial advisor, I have seen firsthand how AI’s integration into various aspects of financial management can significantly benefit clients, streamline operations and enhance decision-making processes. This article explores the multifaceted impact of AI on financial services, backed by practical examples from my professional experience.
Enhancing Investment Strategies With AI
One of the most notable applications of AI in finance is its role in enhancing investment strategies. AI-driven robo-advisors are becoming increasingly popular, providing personalized investment advice based on sophisticated algorithms that analyze vast amounts of data. These robo-advisors consider factors such as market trends, economic indicators and individual client preferences to create tailored investment plans.
For instance, one of my clients, initially skeptical of automated financial tools, decided to allocate a portion of his portfolio to a robo-advisor. This move was part of a diversified investment strategy that balanced traditional financial advisory services with AI-driven insights. Within a year, he observed a 12% increase in his returns, significantly outperforming his manually managed investments. This experience highlights how AI can offer robust, data-driven investment recommendations that adapt to market fluctuations in real time.
Risk Management And Fraud Detection
AI’s ability to process and analyze large datasets at unprecedented speeds has also revolutionized risk management and fraud detection. Financial institutions are leveraging AI to identify potential risks and detect fraudulent activities by analyzing transaction patterns and identifying anomalies that may indicate suspicious behavior.
In my practice, I’ve utilized AI tools to monitor client accounts for unusual activity. For example, a client who frequently traveled internationally faced the risk of unauthorized transactions on his credit cards. By implementing an AI-driven monitoring system, we were able to detect and respond to a fraudulent attempt almost immediately, preventing significant financial loss. This proactive approach not only protects clients’ assets but also enhances their trust in financial advisory services.
Improving Customer Service With AI
Customer service in the financial sector has been significantly improved through the use of AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants. These AI tools can handle a wide range of customer inquiries, from account balances and transaction histories to more complex financial advice, providing 24/7 support and quick resolution of issues.
One practical application involved a client who frequently needed updates on his investment performance but had a busy schedule that made direct communication challenging. By integrating an AI chatbot into our service platform, he could access real-time information about his portfolio and receive timely updates without the need for constant direct interaction. This not only saved time but also ensured he stayed informed about his investments.
AI In Financial Planning And Advisory Services
AI is also transforming financial planning and advisory services by providing advisors with advanced tools to better understand their clients’ needs and goals. AI-driven analytics can assess a client’s financial health, predict future financial scenarios and recommend strategies to achieve long-term financial objectives.
For example, I have used AI-powered financial planning software to help clients visualize different retirement scenarios. By inputting various variables such as income, expenses, savings rate and expected retirement age, I can get the AI tool to generate multiple retirement projections, allowing my clients to see the potential outcomes of different financial strategies. This level of detailed, personalized planning was previously time-consuming and complex, but AI has made it more accessible and accurate.
Challenges And Ethical Considerations
Despite its numerous benefits, the integration of AI in financial services also presents several challenges and ethical considerations. Data privacy is a significant concern, as AI systems require access to vast amounts of personal and financial data to function effectively. Ensuring that this data is securely stored and processed is paramount to maintaining client trust.
Moreover, the reliance on AI algorithms raises questions about transparency and accountability. It is crucial for financial advisors to understand the underlying mechanisms of AI tools to explain their recommendations to clients clearly. Additionally, there is a need for continuous learning and adaptation as AI technology evolves to stay ahead of potential biases and inaccuracies in AI-driven decisions.
The Future Of AI In Financial Services
Looking ahead, the role of AI in financial services is expected to expand further, with ongoing advancements in machine learning, natural language processing and predictive analytics. These technologies will enable even more sophisticated financial products and services, tailored to meet the unique needs of each client.
One emerging trend is the use of AI in environmental, social and governance (ESG) investing. AI can analyze large datasets to assess companies’ ESG performance, helping investors make more informed decisions that align with their values. This is particularly relevant as more investors seek to integrate sustainability into their portfolios.
Another promising area is the use of AI in financial education and literacy. AI-driven platforms can provide personalized financial education resources, helping individuals improve their financial knowledge and make better financial decisions.
Conclusion
In conclusion, AI is undeniably transforming the financial services industry, offering numerous benefits, from enhanced investment strategies and improved risk management to better customer service and personalized financial planning. As an independent financial advisor, embracing these technological advancements has allowed me to provide more comprehensive and efficient services to my clients. However, it is essential to address the associated challenges and ethical considerations to ensure that AI is used responsibly and transparently.
By staying informed about the latest AI developments and continually adapting to new tools and technologies, financial advisors can leverage AI to deliver superior value to their clients, helping them achieve their financial goals in an increasingly complex and dynamic world.
The information provided here is not investment, tax or financial advice. You should consult with a licensed professional for advice concerning your specific situation.

title: Council Post: AI In Design: Dimension Reduction And Emotional Connection
text:
Artin Bogdanov | AI Product Design Leader from Walmart | LinkedIn.
Design is an iterative process of creating a structure and telling a story. The structure provides utility, while the story fosters connection. Although the design process is dynamic, I often find myself addressing two major tasks: dimension reduction and emotional connection. These two aspects are essential in crafting products that are not only functional but also resonate deeply with users.
I’ll explore how dimension reduction enhances the user experience by simplifying interactions and how emotional connection, fueled by AI capabilities, creates meaningful relationships between products and users.
Dimension Reduction
I call it dimension reduction because it quantitatively improves the user experience by reducing interaction dimensions, such as the number of steps, decisions, clicks, time and overall cognitive load in the user’s journey. Dimension reduction is a widely used problem-solving approach in STEM, and design is no exception. As Uncle Rams famously said, “Good design is as little design as possible.”
Dimension reduction inevitably leads to abstraction, which is beneficial because intuitive abstraction drives adoption. We see this in many cases: from Henry Ford’s Model T, which was drastically simplified with fewer parts and less variation, to the iPhone, which initially featured only a single button on the front. Even programming languages have become more accessible as they evolved from low-level, hardware-specific instructions to high-level, human-readable code (such as C, Python and JavaScript), requiring fewer lines of code and fewer architectural considerations.
Generative AI, computer vision and classification machine learning algorithms enable designers to create interfaces that can cut, infer and predict steps throughout the user’s journey. Instead of manually going through all the steps, the system can execute them much faster or even autonomously, asking only for supervision or confirmation instead of requiring the user to perform each step manually. We can see this today in many domains, from autonomous cars and vacuums to facial recognition and image-based credit card entry flows.
The responsibility and opportunity of modern-era designers is to recognize areas for such abstractions and factor them into design solutions. The collection of even small abstractions saves a lot of time, making the overall experience seamless and delightful. It’s like experiencing interface wormholes where you cut interaction spacetime by skipping many otherwise required steps.
That being said, abstraction shouldn’t come at the cost of provided value, especially if it’s a core value of the business. Also, too much abstraction can lead to confusion and might trigger a feeling of lack of control, which might not be preferred in areas where the cost of error is high.
Emotional Connection
Connecting with your users on an emotional level is often more complex than dimension reduction. This qualitative task requires empathy, aesthetics and storytelling skills, all contextualized around the user, brand and value. The goal is to create an integral relationship between the computer interface and the human interacting with it.
The more you know about that human, the better your chances of building such a relationship. That’s why all design processes start with understanding users: their needs, goals, pain points, biases, mental models and environment.
It’s not an easy task and becomes exponentially more difficult with accessibility and localization considerations. Designers, much like investigators, conduct interviews and surveys, create empathy maps and run contextual inquiry sessions to imitate users’ thinking, feelings and actions. Eventually, we get a grasp of whom our users are, what they are trying to achieve and, most importantly, why they are trying to achieve it.
The problem is that there are too many possible persona segmentations. People differ in levels of product familiarity, from first-timers to power users and everything in between. They can follow different job-to-be-done flows, possess various levels of domain expertise and differ in demographics, locations, roles and so on. Not to mention that preferences, needs and expectations change over time as well.
Conventionally, designers deal with this by focusing on a few normalized personas meant to represent all those segments and use cases. This is a somewhat circle-in-a-square approach: It covers a good area but leaves out corner cases, especially at scale. This is where AI/ML technology becomes incredibly helpful, playing an essential role in personalized, empathy-driven design.
Personalization is empathy in action, and AI offers personalization at scale. We designers see empathy as a key component of good design, but its true manifestation lies in providing humans with personalized experiences.
YouTube, Netflix, Spotify, TikTok and many other companies with large value catalogs utilize personalized recommendation algorithms to drive engagement and conversion, making it a central component of their user experience.
That’s why it’s so important for user experience (UX) designers to be aware of AI capabilities and their value. UX designers can leverage this beautiful technology in appropriate places to maximize experience delightfulness and inclusivity, while driving business goals. Therefore, when designing a lengthy list or catalog of options, don’t just default to alphabetical or chronological order. Instead, see if there’s an opportunity to inject AI-enabled personalization.
Conclusion
In the era of artificial intelligence, product design has evolved to balance the quantitative benefits of dimension reduction with the qualitative depth of emotional connection. By reducing interaction dimensions, designers can streamline user experiences, making them more efficient and intuitive.
At the same time, building emotional connections through empathy and personalization ensures that products resonate on a deeper level with users. As AI continues to advance, its role in enhancing both these aspects of design becomes increasingly significant.

title: OpenAI Punches Upward In Bigtime Legal Copyright Lawsuit That Will Surely Determine The Future Longevity Of Generative AI
text:
Put on your everyday armchair legal beagle cap and tighten your seatbelt for a wild ride.
A fierce legal battle involving the future of generative AI took a fascinating turn last week in a tenacious copyright infringement lawsuit that had been brought by a major publisher against AI maker OpenAI of ChatGPT fame. The specific case entails the New York Times (NYT) seeking a legal bid to score a bullseye on OpenAI for scanning and utilizing NYT-posted pieces when creating and data training OpenAI’s litany of generative AI apps including ChatGPT.
This case has profound implications.
To be clear, the likely legal results of this case will be enormous and ultimately apply to just about all AI makers and all generative AI apps, thus each and every chess move during the case portends bigtime implications. The future of generative AI is at stake. Yes, that might seem like an overstatement, but for various reasons that I’ll get into shortly, the potential ramifications aren’t that far off from what could go down.
I’ll get to the earth-shattering latest twist in a moment, so hang in there, it’s a worthy doozy.
First, some quick stage-setting remarks.
For those of you generally interested in the legal ins and outs of what’s happening with AI, you might find highly informative and engaging my comprehensive coverage at the link here. In the heady matter of Intellectual Property rights and AI, such as copyrights and patents, my analyses at the link here and the link here would provide handy insights for you. Other coverage includes the controversial proposition of legal personhood rights for AI, see the link here, plus many other pieces that I’ve posted as part of my ongoing examination of the latest in AI Law and AI Ethics, see the link here.
Let’s next unpack the newsworthy aspects that recently took place.
Return Of The Jedi Or The Empire Strikes Back
In case you aren’t aware of the broad notion at play, OpenAI, like many other major AI makers, has generally skirted around paying for or even asking permission to do scanning of posted works on the Internet that are copyrighted. The AI makers would tend to conveniently argue that this is perfectly fine. People read the same content and analyze in their minds what the material says, thus, data training of generative AI should readily be allowed to do the same thing. Period, end of story.
The counterargument by publishers and copyright owners is that the AI makers are doing an overt and improper “taking” of posted content. This is being done without permission being granted by the rightful legal owners. Furthermore, AI makers are making tons of dough from having done the considered illicit scanning, for which the publishers and copyright owners are being left out of the massive pot of gold thereof.
You’ve got publishers and copyright owners crowing that AI makers are villainous and want to greedily steal what’s not rightfully theirs to then profit from. Outrageous. Smacks of days of the Wild West. A slew of lawsuits has been launched. It is somewhat of a slow grind. The war for online data is waging at a snail’s pace in our courts, meanwhile, generative AI apps are being advanced and produced at the speed of newborn bunny rabbits.
The AI makers would insist that if anyone posts content on the Internet for people to read, it is fair game for being read. Just because the publisher or copyright owner hasn’t found additional ways to garner revenue from their works doesn’t mean that enterprising alternative approaches should have to fork over anything, not even a dime. If you put your stuff out there on the web for ready display and consumption by humans, well, by gosh, it is logically reasonable to assert that AI can do the same.
A few months ago, a Harvard Law Review blog entitled “NYT v. OpenAI: The Times’s About Face” by Audrey Pope, April 10, 2024, made these salient points overall about this particular legal battle at hand (excerpts):
- “The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft for the unpermitted use of Times articles to train GPT large language models.”
- “These tools are large language models (LLMs), which are built by “training” on massive corpora of text.”
- “At the root of the Times’s complaint is that this dataset contains a “mass of Times copyrighted content.”
- “The Times’s core allegation is that OpenAI is infringing on copyrights through the unlicensed and unauthorized use and reproduction of Times works during the training of its models.”
- “The case could have a significant impact on the relationship between generative AI and copyright law, particularly with respect to fair use, and could ultimately determine whether and how AI models are built.”
I trust that you get the gist of the considerations underway.
The Whole Kit And Kaboodle Is At Stake
When I bring up this weighty topic at AI conferences during my various speeches and presentations, some instantly tune out because they falsely assume that this is just a lot of arcane legal wrangling and only a topic of importance to AI nerds and the lawyers who make money from what AI nerds do.
There’s more at stake, a lot more.
Assume that generative AI is a powerhouse form of AI that will continue to permeate our daily lives at home, at work, and play. Generative AI is becoming ubiquitous. It is sometimes used on a standalone basis, such as the use of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Bard, and so on, while in many other instances, generative AI is baked into other applications. Nearly all kinds of apps will eventually have a connection to a generative AI app. This might be on the backend, and you won’t overtly access it, but the generative AI is there under the hood and being fully relied upon.
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
By and large, the massive amount of data that has been used to devise generative AI apps has come at nearly zero cost for the AI makers. That’s right, I said a near-zero cost. Other than the cost of their software and servers needed to do the scanning of the Internet, they rarely have paid a cent for the actual content being scanned. All those colossal volumes of data were needed to bring generative AI into the condition or computational state that we now know as being relatively fluent in the patterning of human writing.
They got it for next to nothing.
Data is so vital to the ongoing advancement of generative AI that an overwhelming worry is afoot about whether there is enough data on the Internet to sustain the growth of generative AI, see my analysis at the link here. The concern is that with the AI makers scraping at the bottom of the barrel and finding every conceivable nook and cranny of the Internet, they will run out of data at some point (conjecture ranges from within 5 years to others saying it is more like by the year 2050). A voiced alternative involves having generative AI produce data, known as synthetic data, and feed that into generative AI for additional training, which some fear will lead to what is referred to as a catastrophic model collapse, see my discussion at the link here.
Some people liken data to oil. They proclaim that the need for and search for data is analogous to the pursuit of oil. We all realize that modern-day machinery such as cars, planes, and so on are dependent on the availability of oil. Oil is what makes the world turn, so they say. The idea is that data is what makes generative AI work. Oil is a precious commodity. So, it is said, is data.
No data, no generative AI.
Remedies Could Kill The Golden Goose
Consider what the present-day lawsuits against AI makers portend.
Suppose the courts decide that AI makers did a virtual rip-off and now must pay publishers and copyright owners some compensatory pay for what has transpired. Notice that this is not simply about a go-forward basis of payment. The idea is that the water under the bridge must also be paid for. All that data that was already scanned ought to spur a monetary reimbursement to the publishers and copyright owners.
No problem, you might be thinking, those AI makers have been rolling in dough and they certainly can afford a few pennies here and there to be tossed to the publishers and copyright owners. I dare say the idea is that this is going to be a lot more than spare change. The aim of some of the publishers and copyright owners is that truly big bucks are owed. In addition, significant financial penalties ought to be assessed. Think of it as the interest owed on the non-voluntary non-approved loan of that data, for which an after-the-fact pricing should ding the AI makers to serve as a wake-up call for their said-to-be outrageous intrusion and unapologetic transgression.
Some say that this could wipe out the AI makers and we would end up with generative AI apps that eat the dust.
The existing generative AI apps might barely be kept going, limping along at best. The AI would no longer be advanced since the cost of the data has outpriced what can be paid. Akin to the analogy of data to oil, if oil becomes too high priced, the rest of the world that depends upon oil to run machinery dries up too. Generative AI would summarily dry up as a result of sky-high pricing of available data (that’s partially why the idea of substituting cheap-to-produce synthetic data is so profoundly being avidly pursued, see my discussion at the link here).
Another angle of what could happen to AI makers is that if the AI makers aren’t willing to pay up or wish fervently to avert doing so, at least they should be legally compelled to remove anything in their respective generative AI app that relied upon the scanning of said copyright-protected data. It seems easy-peasy. If the generative AI app used this or that copyrighted data during scanning, merely go into the generative AI and excise any aspects that relied upon that data. Removal is a considered cure of sorts.
As I’ve covered at the link here, the removal of all and any internal facets that are interconnected to particular data scans is a huge chore and pretty much highly technologically problematic to try and pull off. A lot of research is taking place on so-called “unlearning” with respect to generative AI. Progress is slow. It is a tough problem to solve, a hard nut to crack.
The odds are that such removal would be costly, assuming it could be done on a large scale. It would also be unlikely to get everything, and residual aspects would remain. Worse still, the result is likely to undercut the generative AI such that it will have been shredded to pieces and no longer operate at all like it did before the shish kabob was undertaken.
One viewpoint is that the AI makers might as well scrap what they’ve devised and start anew, beginning fresh from scratch and making sure this time to do deals with publishers and copyright owners (you’ve likely seen in the news that those deals are already being made, partially to cope with the sordid past that looms over the AI makers, and partially to make the future path less filled with legal potholes and gotchas). Starting over has a lot of downsides, ergo, it isn’t a magic wand or silver bullet. Far from it.
A retort is that we ought to not shed a tear or play even a teensy tiny sad violin for the AI makers.
They got themselves into this jam. They gladly or perhaps gleefully scanned data that they either knew or ought to have known was copyright protected. They should have asked for permission at the get-go. Instead, they decided to take what they wanted first and answer questions later. Classic audacious behavior of those overconfident ego-laden AI wizards. The risks were high, and they figured it was something to deal with someday, maybe, if they eventually got caught with their hands in the cookie jar.
So far, they have had their cake and been eating it too. Someday, the cheating chickens must come home to roost and face the consequences. That’s what some publishers and copyright owners proclaim is the basis for their court cases.
Wait for a second, the reply comes, this is going to be shooting our own foot on a societal-wide scope.
We are becoming highly dependent on generative AI. If the AI makers can’t keep generative AI going or not advancing, the hoped-for cures to cancer from generative AI aren’t going to materialize. Society is going to be set back on its heels. Generative AI has become too big and too important to allow it to falter or fail.
The whole matter indeed seems chillingly like a game of chicken, whereby publishers and copyright owners are driving squarely at AI makers, and the AI makers are driving squarely at them, for which a massive and consequential car crash with everyone involved seems to be at play. Will everyone get hurt? Will only one side get hurt? Will no one get hurt?
Nobody can say for sure.
The Essence Of Copyright Is The Key Factor
Returning to the legal battles that are underway, the crux is whether the data-training associated with modern-day generative AI and the scanning and use of Internet data that is copyrighted shall be considered a violation of copyright laws.
This seemingly can end up in one of two ways.
If the courts decide that generative AI, as devised today, doesn’t infringe, AI makers will be ecstatic and presumably popping bottles of champagne. Publishers and copyright owners will indubitably believe they are being unfairly ripped off and the courts have failed to ensure the proper protection of their hard-earned Intellectual Property rights. Sad face.
On the other hand, if the courts decide that generative AI, as devised today, does infringe, the next question will be one of what form and approach should be taken regarding making whole those whose copyrights were violated. This is likely to be on a case-by-case basis, though prior tangential precedents will likely come into the picture, as would whatever initial keystone cases opt to establish precedents in this specific neck of the woods.
AI makers will obviously be upset if they lose on this. You can expect legal appeals to be made by them and this will drag on in the courts for years to come (perhaps it will be settled by the time we reach sentient AI, and at that point, all bets are off anyway).
Settlement negotiations will be likely in the offing, for which the publisher or copyright owner will now have added leverage with the win being in their hands. In that sense, there is an eyeball-to-eyeball gambit already underway of whether AI makers should try to settle the existing legal cases now or wait and see. Money is potentially in hand right now for the copyright owners, which might be nice, but likely not as much a bonanza for money down the road apace if wins occur decidedly.
A roll of the dice is involved.
The consequences overall will be cascading if the infringement claim prevails. First, the winner of a particular legal battle will seek to extract some form of payment from the AI maker found to be an infringer. Second, other publishers and copyright owners that haven’t launched a legal case will be emboldened to do so. A rush to the money trough will ensue. Other AI makers that may be under the radar right now will also become new targets for lawsuits and/or dialogues about making settlements before going the court route. The winner that took one AI maker to task will look around to see which other AI makers are likely infringers too.
And so on, the ball bounces, as they say.
The zillion-dollar question then that we must think mindfully about is whether generative AI devised in the manner prescribed is in fact a form of copyright infringement.
What do you think?
I’d say we should take a closer look. The first place to give scrutiny is what constitutes copyrights, copyright infringement, and related elements.
Here’s a handy definition of copyright in the U.S.:
- “Copyright infringement is the unauthorized use of another’s work. This is a legal issue that depends on whether or not the work is protected by copyright in the first place, as well as on specifics like how much is used and the purpose of the use. If one copies too much of a protected work, or copies for an unauthorized purpose, simply acknowledging the original source will not solve the problem. Only by seeking prior permission from the copyright holder does one avoid the risk of an infringement charge” (Duke University School of Law, website posting).
Let’s see how that definition pertains to generative AI and the production of generative AI outputs.
Generative AI is customarily devised to do pattern-matching when performing initial data training. In a sense, a template of what humans write about is constructed via scanning lots and lots of essays. Furthermore, usually, a probabilistic or statistical approach is used when generating an essay or text as output. This helps in producing what seems to be wholly unique new essays or text outputs each time that you ask a question of AI or enter a prompt. Otherwise, each time an essay or text output was generated, it might look word-for-word exactly the same as a prior output that the AI had generated.
There is a potential problem though.
You see, sometimes the pattern-matching will end up not as a template but instead as a word-for-word digital copy of something that was scanned. This might then on a verbatim basis be later produced as an output, and the AI will have pretty much showcased an outright exact copy of the scanned content. Dicey territory that stridently suggests nearly blatant infringement of copyrighted content that was scanned (and not otherwise licensed or done with the explicit permission of the copyright owner).
That is one Achilles heel for AI makers and their generative AI apps.
Must Be Copyrighted And Must Be Copyrightable
We are now getting nearer to the important twist that I alluded to earlier.
The rule of thumb is that a copyrighted work must be copyrighted, such as filing for an official government copyright certification, and must also be copyrightable. Here’s what that means. You decide to take a story you wrote and proceed to formally obtain a copyright for it (there is also an implied copyright aspect, which I won’t go into here, see my discussion at the link here).
Happily, you get the official copyright certification and believe you have done everything you need to do. Turns out you might not be as peachy keen as you assumed. Anyway, some months later, a third party comes along, and they have written a story that appears to infringe on your copyright.
You decide to sue them for infringement.
They would likely first want to see proof that your work was copyrighted, along with when it was copyrighted and any other facets that might mar your assertion that it is copyrighted. That’s a line of attack any lawyer worth their salt would readily undertake. Undercut the copyright and thus curtail or undercut the claim of infringement.
Another viable line of attack is whether your claimed-to-be copyrighted content is copyrightable. If it isn’t copyrightable, you are in a tough posture. Suppose for example that your story is actually a word-for-word copy of a story that someone else wrote. Let’s say that your story violates or infringes on someone else’s copyright (and assume that this is not legally shakable, though I’m sure you would try). You in a sense do not have something copyrightable, despite your belief that you did, even though you registered the content and got a copyright certification.
You are hurting now.
I would like to emphasize that I am simplifying the nature of copyrights and there is a lot of additional complexity. I urge you to make sure you have a good Intellectual Property rights lawyer to aid you in sufficiently protecting any content that you have. Copyright is a byzantine affair, that’s for darned sure.
For example, there are various limitations associated with how far copyright law extends, consider these crucial points:
- “Copyright does not protect ideas, only the specific expression of an idea. For example, a court decided that Dan Brown did not infringe the copyright of an earlier book when he wrote The Da Vinci Code because all he borrowed from the earlier work were the basic ideas, not the specifics of plot or dialogue. Since copyright is intended to encourage creative production, using someone else’s ideas to craft a new and original work upholds the purpose of copyright, it does not violate it. Only if one copies another’s expression without permission is copyright potentially infringed” (Duke University School of Law, website posting).
There are numerous permissible exceptions for legally being able to copy copyrighted materials, as this cited note from the U.S. Copyright Office website mentions (excerpt):
- “The Copyright Act’s exceptions and limitations found in sections 107-122 include fair use, the “first sale doctrine,” some reproductions by libraries and archives, certain performances and displays, broadcast programming transmissions by cable and satellite, to name a few. Interested in more information on fair use? Take a look at our Fair Use Index. The complete list of exemptions to copyright protection can be found in Chapter 1 of Title 17 of the United States Code. You can also use works that are in the public domain. Works in the public domain are those that are never protected by copyright (like facts or discoveries) or works whose term of protection has ended either because it expired, or the owner did not satisfy a previously required formality. Currently, all pre-1926 U.S. works are in the public domain because copyright protection has expired for those works” (U.S. Copyright Office website).
You might have observed in that cited description that items considered in the public domain can be usually used without invoking a copyright violation.
Here’s how that comes up regarding generative AI.
Some AI makers will at times try to confine their generative AI to being data trained on solely works that are in the public domain and that are also in online stock libraries that they have been licensed to use. All in all, the goal is to only data train on content that there is little or no chance of garnering a copyright infringement upon. If your generative AI-produced item is identical to a public domain item, you presumably are in the clear. If your generative AI-produced item is identical to the online stock library item that was licensed by the AI maker, you are presumably in the clear if you abide by whatever other stipulations the AI maker has imposed about doing such copying (make sure to closely review the licensing agreement of the generative AI app).
You can certainly give a loud cheer that this data-training approach will help matters.
Questions arise such as whether enough such data is available. Another factor is the cost of paying for the online stock libraries' access and use of their copyrighted materials. The relative dearth of public domain data and the exorbitant cost of getting access to priced data might not be sufficient to craft generative AI worthy of our rapt attention. It will be menial in comparison to the generative AI we are solidly accustomed to now. That dismal ho-hum generative AI is essentially worthless or useless generative AI.
Okay, so let’s say that scanning copyrighted data is to be generally allowed (we will decree this), but make sure that the generative AI doesn’t go overboard and can’t land on a word-by-word basis as a copycat. Just glance at the copyrighted essays and texts, do pattern matching at an arms-length distance, and be done with this whole assorted conniption.
Sorry, that’s not so good either.
Recall that the definition used above about copyright is that you can be an infringer even if you don’t entirely and precisely copy the copyrighted item. The indication was that if “one copies too much of a protected work” is where you can get into trouble. This is a loosey-goosey realm, and legal arguments will likely be made by opposing parties that either too much of a protected work was copied or the copying fell below an argued threshold.
The advent of generative AI has raised a slew of thorny questions about copyright laws.
Maybe we need to refine existing laws to take into account generative AI aspects. Some exhort that an overhaul of copyright laws is overdue, and that generative AI is a welcome trigger to do so. Some believe that no new laws and no changes to laws are required. They believe that traditional copyright laws are fully applicable and handle the gamut of anything generative AI legally raises.
Messy, messy, messy.
Recent Salvo By OpenAI In The New York Times Case
In the existing legal case of the NYT claiming copyright infringement by OpenAI, the parties are currently in the discovery phase. You likely know about legal discovery in general due to all manner of high-profile court cases shown on live streams or made available as recorded video on social media (plus via plentiful fictional movies and TV shows that semi-realistically depict legal cases).
Each side tries to get the other side to show what it has, almost like playing a poker game and you hope to discover what cards the other side is holding.
The judge often must make difficult decisions about requests by either side. Not everything that is requested will necessarily be legally applicable and the judge will turn down such requests. The sides typically try to get what they believe will be in their best interest, serving as a strenuous advocate for their side of the case. They will pitch or make legal arguments that the judge reviews and then the judge decides or rules whether the various requests can go forward, including the extent to which a given request must be fulfilled by the other side of the case.
Keep that in mind as we explore the recent filings.
Tighten your seatbelt.
OpenAI made a filing on July 1, 2024, that is publicly available about the ongoing discovery process and provides a useful glimpse at the back-and-forth going on during the present-day discovery phase of the case. I am going to provide some quoted excerpts from that filing (this is in the case of “The New York Times Company v. Microsoft Corp., et al.”, Case No. 1:23-cv-11195-SHS). I will do the same when showcasing excerpts from the response filed by the NYT lawyers, dated July 3, 2024.
If this complex legal matter interests you, please make sure to read the entire filings of both parties to suitably grasp the entirety of the discovery matters currently being addressed. Be aware that I am going to select just a few highlights here or there.
Here’s a stated indication in the July 1, 2024 filing of why OpenAI is requesting various materials from NYT as part of the discovery process (excerpt):
- “Discovery into those copyrighted works is directly relevant both to the Times’s claim of copyright infringement and to OpenAI’s defenses (such as fair use, which looks at, inter alia, various aspects of the works at issue). The Times can only assert infringement over those portions of the works that are (a) original to the author, and (b) owned or exclusively licensed to the Times.” (ibid).
I trust that you can see that OpenAI posits there is a sound basis for their discovery request, namely that they are seeking materials from NYT to examine whether the claimed-to-be infringed works are copyrightable and copyrighted.
OpenAI seems to be seeking specifics about how the works at issue were devised by NYT. Thus, the expressed need to be able to inspect the reporter’s notes, materials that were used in formulating the works, and other related aspects (excerpt):
- “Any ambiguity was resolved during the parties’ conferrals when OpenAI explained that it was seeking “underlying reporter’s notes, interview memos, records of materials cited, or other ‘files’ for each asserted work.” (ibid).
Furthermore, OpenAI states that this is a bona fide request for these additional reasons (excerpt):
- “Such discovery is also relevant to other assertions the Times has made, including those regarding how the Times created the works at issue. The Times alleges, for example, that “[t]o produce world-class journalism,” it “invests an enormous amount of time, . . . expertise, and talent,” including through “deep investigations—which usually take months and sometimes years to report and produce—into complex and important areas of public interest.” Compl. ¶¶ 32–33; see also id. ¶¶ 34–37. Having chosen to put directly at issue how the Times created the works at issue—including the methods, time, labor, and investment—OpenAI has a right to discovery into the same.” (ibid).
The bottom line is that the request seeks to get the inner workings that went into the development of the copyrighted works at play.
Does that seem innocuous and uneventful? Or does it seem possibly outlandish and a bridge too far? Should the judge approve the request or deny it? What would be the basis for approving the request versus denying the request?
Questions abound.
Take a moment to reflect on this from both sides of the case at hand.
There is something about this that from a publisher's perspective is potentially unsettling and would make them shudder and shake. Those qualms are due to the possibility that a publisher or copyright owner will legally need to open the kimono, as it were, and reveal their deepest darkest secrets about how they put together their published works. As you likely know, an ongoing struggle has persisted over protecting journalists from outside inquiries and ensuring the sanctity of freedom of the press. This is a conundrum that society has been toiling over since the writing of the Constitution (before that, too).
Even if privileged facets could somehow be excluded, would the unveiling of the nitty gritty that goes into composing news stories potentially reflect poorly on a publisher and its journalists? It might be akin to going into a diner and walking into the backroom to see how the food is being prepared and cooked. Sometimes that’s just fine, sometimes it can be unnerving.
What do you think the NYT lawyers would say to this attempt at a piercing of the veil?
In the rejoinder on behalf of the NYT, dated July 3, 2024, and publicly available for this court case, they responded with some hard-hitting responses.
Here’s an excerpt:
- “OpenAI’s claim that it needs all “reporter’s notes, interview memos, records of materials cited, or other ‘files’ for each asserted work”—purportedly to determine whether The Times’s works are in fact protectable intellectual property—is unprecedented and turns copyright law on its head. OpenAI cites no caselaw permitting such invasive discovery, and for good reason. It is far outside the scope of what’s allowed under the Federal Rules and serves no purpose other than harassment and retaliation for The Times’s decision to file this lawsuit.” (ibid).
They go on to say this too:
- “Permitting OpenAI to investigate The Times’s privileged newsgathering process would have serious negative and far-reaching consequences. It would entail the disclosure of The Times’s confidential reporters’ files on investigative reporting into highly sensitive matters, including those related to the Defendants themselves. OpenAI’s request imposes an undue burden on The Times that is disproportionate to (and indeed, wholly divorced from) the needs of this case.” (ibid).
And, in rather provocative language, they emphasize this:
- “The Court should reject OpenAI’s effort to weaponize discovery as a means of targeting the confidential and irrelevant information that underpins The Times’s reporting. The Times’s newsgathering process is not on trial. OpenAI and Microsoft’s infringement of millions of The Times’s registered copyright works is.”
Yikes, that’s a tad smarmy.
So it goes, in love, war, and legal battles.
If you’d like to see my coverage of how things have gotten noticeably ugly in the act of so-called lawfare, including the role of AI and especially generative AI, see the link here.
Back to the tit-for-tat.
In the July 1 filing by OpenAI, they had generally anticipated a legal rebuff and had stated preemptively that (excerpts):
- “To begin with, the New York Shield Law does not apply because this case does not involve a claim under state law.” (ibid).
- “And the reporters’ privilege under federal law does not justify withholding the materials at issue here because they (i) are of likely relevance to a significant issue in the case—whether the Times is asserting copyright protection over works or portions thereof in which it does not have a copyright—and (ii) are not reasonably obtainable from other available sources.” (ibid).
On and on this goes in both filings. I believe you get the general drift.
The parties also argue about other facets such as copyright certifications, but I anticipate that those disputes will get somewhat squarely resolved. The other elements aren’t quite of the same degree of contention and magnitude. Revealing how the sausage is made, well, that’s the 600-pound gorilla in the courtroom.
This glimpse at just two filings is a mere drop in the bucket of the customary head-to-head legal strategies and tactics that arise as numerous chess moves and counter moves occur in a case of this significance. There is a lot on the line. These are heavyweights going toe-to-toe. The consequences are enormous for them, and notably too, for the future of generative AI.
From a layman’s viewpoint, that is going to be a humongous sticky wicket.
The Big Wow Of Why This Is Demonstrably Important
Let’s now do some freewheeling on why the point about possibly being required to reveal reporters' notes and other materials is so frothy and contentious.
One perspective is that if this specific court case proceeds to enforce such a request, presumably other akin cases will leap on the bandwagon and potentially do so too. This could be good or bad, depending on your viewpoint. All of a sudden, lots of journalists might find themselves having to legally reveal facets of their reporting that heretofore were believed to be protected from view.
You might assert that there are already narrow exceptions to the rule, but then again, the question arises whether “merely” satisfying copyright infringement is a high enough and important enough cause to take such a bold step. Some would exhort that you are opening a Pandora's box. How so? Creative sneaky types might proceed to bring copyright lawsuits principally to get at the journalist's notes, whereas the copyright concerns of the case itself are of lesser consequence to them. It is a kind of Trojan horse.
That covers the slippery slope conundrum that comes to mind.
Another would be the potential embarrassment and reputational damage that might accrue to the publisher or copyright owner. If the public at large believes that the journalists work diligently and with extreme care, but if the notes and materials suggest otherwise, that’s a dark day for those journalists and the field journalism all told (it is already abundantly under scrutiny, heaven knows).
Maybe those points are leaning you in the direction of saying that such a request is unwarranted.
Hold onto your hat, let’s see what the other viewpoint might be.
If generative AI is potentially going to be pummeled into the ground via copyrights, and if we in our heart-of-hearts fully believe that generative AI provides a lot of public good, you would want to presumably be absolutely sure that copyright infringement has truly occurred. If the copyright is invalid for whatever legal reason, every stone should be overturned to show why that’s the case. Do not let a shallow review determine the fate of generative AI.
In terms of reputational damage, that’s a matter on the shoulders of those who perform the journalistic work. The deal is this. If the emperor doesn’t really have any clothes, the public ought to not be hoodwinked to believe otherwise. Professional journalists should be willing to hold their heads high and be proud of the work they do. Not just in the results, but by openly displaying the thoroughness and trustworthiness of how the results were derived.
Is that leaning you back in this other direction?
All in all, you can see that this is a tough decision to make. Each side has a compelling legal argument. Each side derides the other side as not having a compelling legal argument. And so it goes. Just another day in the vigorously adversarial field of law.
The Twist Upon The Twist Is Not Very Clean
I’ve now walked you step-by-step to the final moment of truth.
Are you ready?
Yet another intriguing viewpoint is whether getting publishers to show their underlying work might reveal something else of keen interest to this specific legal matter on the use of generative AI.
I will describe this as what’s good for the goose is good for the gander. Or, similarly, you can go ahead and phrase it as what’s bad for the goose is bad for the gander.
The deal is this.
There is a legal doctrine known as having unclean hands. The idea is pretty apparent and goes this way. If a party has performed some form of shall we say misconduct, their ability to stand tall is undercut. Their hands are not clean. They must pay the price accordingly. If both parties to a matter have unclean hands, a kind of parity could potentially be said to exist. Perhaps they both can be told to walk away, keeping the status quo intact, because neither party was in the clear.
Here's a formal definition of this legal construct entailing clean hands and unclean hands (excerpt):
- “The clean-hands doctrine is the principle that a party’s own inequitable misconduct precludes recovery based on equitable claims or defenses. The doctrine requires that a party act fairly in the matter for which they seek a remedy. A party who has violated an equitable principle, such as good faith, is described as having "unclean hands.” The clean-hands doctrine is invoked when a party seeking equitable relief or claiming a defense based in equity has themselves violated a duty of good faith or has acted unconscionably in connection with the same subject matter out of which they claim a right to relief.” (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, “Clean-Hands Doctrine” posting).
A crucial U.S. Supreme Court case in 1945 set the ground rules for this doctrine (excerpt):
- "This maxim is far more than a mere banality. It is a self-imposed ordinance that closes the doors of a court of equity to one tainted with inequitableness or bad faith relative to the matter in which he seeks relief, however improper may have been the behavior of the defendant. That doctrine is rooted in the historical concept of the court of equity as a vehicle for affirmatively enforcing the requirements of conscience and good faith. U.S. Supreme Court, Precision Instrument Mfg. Co. v. Automotive Maintenance Machinery Co., 324 U.S. 806, 1945).
Various other legal cases have refined the scope and nature of the doctrine, such as generally indicating that the question of clean hands or unclean hands is supposed to be pertinent to the keystone of the matter and not at the peripheral outskirts (excerpts):
- “The doctrine of unclean hands does not deny relief to a plaintiff guilty of any past misconduct; only misconduct directly related to the matter in which he seeks relief triggers the defense.” Kendall-Jackson Winery v. Superior Court, 76 Cal. App. 4th 970, Cal. Ct. App., 1999).
How does this fit to generative AI?
Imagine this. I want you to step away from any existing court case. Do a thought experiment with me.
Generative AI is data trained on lots of seemingly copyrighted material on the Internet. This has the appearance of unclean hands. Suppose that upon further scrutiny, the material that was said to be copyrighted had followed the same kind of leveraging and leaning into other copyrighted materials to devise the content now being contested as to being scanned and violating copyrights. Humans, perhaps in the role of reporters or journalists, let’s say they went around and “scanned” lots of copyrighted materials and then in their minds rejiggered it into seemingly copyrighted content.
Could we perhaps say that this is yet another instance of unclean hands?
We might see this as both opposing parties having unclean hands. If so, the one claiming to have been harmed by copyright infringement has done essentially the same that those they accuse have done. Sure, one might be by human cognition, while the other by mathematical and computational AI efforts, but they both presumably commingle together copyrighted prior works to make their presumed proclaimed copyrightable works.
Think about that.
There are points and counterpoints, which I’ll save for another posting since I’m running long on this discussion.
Conclusion
Is the legal matter of generative AI and copyrights a simple issue that is obvious to the eye, or does it entail layers upon layers of intricate considerations involving legal, societal, cultural, and ethical provisions?
Welcome to an onerous debate that has significant implications.
Here are some final thoughts to contemplate with a glass of fine wine.
A famous line by English jurist John Selden said this: “Ignorance of the law excuses no one.”
The publishers and copyright owners would undoubtedly vehemently argue that though the AI makers might have been unaware of their having violated copyright laws (which, to the publishers and copyright owners stretches credulity beyond belief), in any case, this proffers no excuse for what they have done. Make them pay. Get to the quick and move on.
Roman statement Marcus Tullius Cicero indicated this vital remark: “The good of the people is the highest law.”
If AI makers indeed have scanned copyrighted works, and the result is amazingly fluent generative AI that aids in solving many key problems facing humankind, and if this is leading us to some more advanced form of AI such as Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) that will dramatically transform and uplift how humans live and work, wouldn’t we be remiss in clamping down at this juncture?
The price to compensate copyright holders might disrupt and curtail the furtherance of generative AI. It is as though we were on the path to landing on the moon and scuttled the trip on a technicality. Our eyes need to be on the prize that is down the road. Don’t let short-term indulgences distract us from the long-term upsides.
There you have two opposing views.
As an armchair judge, go ahead and make your decision.
One other aspect, when it comes to the law and making decisions based on the law, please remember the renowned words of Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., considered one of the greatest legal minds of all time, in which he plainly said this: “The law is a living thing.”
May we all live and learn in harmony.
Stay tuned for my ongoing coverage on this and many other pressing topics about the latest in AI.

title: Retail This Week: Soft Landings, AI Hype, And Department Store Deaths
text:
The phrase ‘soft landing’ is back in the news descriptions, after signs from all across the world of cooling labor markets, cooling inflation, and more soft consumer spending. In retail tech data, two related stories about how much product information consumers can take. I have one AI story that doesn’t really sound like a bunch of AI, and one question based on a Meta ad about AI. We’ll round out with one “I told you so”, one good question with a bad answer, and three immersive retail stories (though one includes Roblox). Let’s dive in!
Retail Economic Indicators
Different countries, with their different governments, economic policies, and business climates, have experienced differing levels of impact from the forces driving the post-pandemic global economy. And yet, as much as there are differences, the dominating forces are all the same: inflation, a tight labor market, and uncertainty driven first by supply chain disruptions and then by geopolitical ones.
Support for this idea comes from three different stories from three different parts of the world. First up, the US Bureau of Labor and Statistics served up a lukewarm labor market. Total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 206,000 in June, and the unemployment rate climbed ever so slightly to 4.1%. When you look at the trend line, it seems to be starting a slow and steady climb basically since March. And the job gains for April-May-June have been lower than the three preceding months. Jobs beat analyst expectations, but this quote sums it up: “Things are not too hot and not too cold. Goldilocks is here…”
Retail sales in Australia have had a tougher time than other markets, but even there managed to turn in lukewarm sales improvements. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, May retail sales increased 1.5% year over year, which is not enough to outpace inflation. But discretionary spending was the bright spot – clothing, footwear, and personal accessories notched the biggest gains.
Meanwhile in the UK, retail store prices continue to ease off, posting an 0.2% increase in June, according to the British Retail Consortium in partnership with NielsenIQ. Non-food prices actually fell 1%, down from -0.8% the preceding month.
Retail Tech & Research Data
I could have flipped a coin to decide in which order to tell you about these next two studies. GS1 US conducted a consumer study and found out that 77% of consumers believe product information is important when making a purchase and 79% of shoppers are more likely to purchase products with a QR code that offers the information they’re looking for. GS1 published the study as part of an effort to promote Sunrise 2027, which involves brands transitioning off of UPCs and on to QR or 2D barcodes on product and packaging. Retailers need to be ready to accept them for checkout scans by 2027.
And yet! Consumers may actually have too much product information, so much so that they abandon all carts. But of course, AI can help. Accenture drove this study, finding that 75% of consumers have abandoned a shopping cart in the last three months due to feeling “bombarded by content, overwhelmed by choice, and frustrated by the amount of effort they need to put into making decisions.” The study concluded that 74% if retail sales are at risk due to information overload. The article then describes an effort by Unilever that uses a “proprietary generative AI tool that auto-updates product descriptions on digital commerce sites” in response to the search trends on each site. It’s live now on up to 10 markets (including the US).
This application of GenAI is cool – and something that you couldn’t do today because it would take too long and require too much effort to maintain it. However, what that has to do with consumers feeling information overload, I have no idea. Consumers have too much information at their disposal, and it’s so overwhelming that it can actually cause them not to buy (I am certainly guilty of “Ugh, I’m not going to make this decision right now” and abandoning a cart), even though they find it extremely valuable, if not central to the shopping experience. GS1 wants to put brands more directly in control of what information is available to consumers and Accenture wants brands to use GenAI to better control how that information is made available to customers. Both of these are interesting things but don’t really solve the central question: how do you make it easier for consumers to decide? Not just how to force them to pick you.
AI & Retail
That last article could’ve crossed over into this section, but it did lead with a consumer study, so I stuck it there. Instead, I want to look at two sides of the same coin. On one side, everything is AI these days. And some AI is not quite so groundbreaking because it has been around long enough that it just doesn’t have the impact it used to. I think Ben Evans says “Anything innovative is AI, until it’s just software.”
In this case, MatsukiyoCocokara has started leveraging the AI-driven Revieve Platform to put out a digital skincare advisor, a virtual try-on, and a digital haircare advisor. In stores, staff will have tablets to offer personalized recommendations. Online, you can access the experience with your phone by leveraging (what else?) a QR code.
The AI here is old school – it’s camera vision coupled with some personalization software. I would feel more impressed if MatsukiyoCocokara has an infinite number of custom products to recommend but I doubt that’s the case. Most beauty companies have eight, or ten, or if you’re Fenty, 57. But there is still a finite number, and most of the variation is about finding the right shade, not the right composition. So it’s kind of like using a complex Rube Goldberg-like machine to spit out what might basically be a roll of the dice. Or just a quick peek at some predominating characteristics – oh, your hair is dry and fine? That’s formula #3. Which a human could do just as easily. Yes, camera vision is AI. But also, not the kind of personalization that the hype is setting people up to expect.
Then there’s the new Meta ad, touting AI as some kind of life enhancer. But the questions people are asking are exactly the fear of what happens if the hype deflates. Build me a training program? What should I do if I have to plant a sun-loving plant in a greenhouse? In the early days of the hype (yes, it has been around long enough to have ‘early days’), someone said using ChatGPT to write you a cover letter is like using a Lamborghini to deliver a pizza. I can see that Meta is trying to pry share away from OpenAI, but this is the best we can come up with for how AI is going to change our lives? That’s some scary evidence that this is way over-hyped.
Retail Winners and Losers
Every once in a while I get to say “I told you so” and it’s never more gratifying than when it’s something related to a trend I called out as having the potential to impact 2024. This article from Retail Brew describes how Lowe’s and Unilever are gearing up to refocus away from price increases and more towards winning back shoppers who are defecting away from high prices. We’ve seen this happening during the first half of 2024. There was always the fear that at some point shoppers would start trading down, and in 2024, they finally did – noticeably so, and especially noticed by the retailers that consumers were trading away from. Price increases are getting harder and harder to pull off, and for retailers who could once lose share but make it up in margins, they have to find a new strategy, one that wins those shoppers back.
It will be an interesting experiment in rebuilding brand trust. Everyone always says it’s cheaper to retain a customer than to lose one and try to win them back. I guess we’ll find out if that is true. The most interesting point in the article is that while retailers and brands are returning to trying to win volume, their ad dollars are not returning to pre-pandemic marketing channels. Digital advertising and loyalty program incentives are the two big winners.
I wish I didn’t get to say I told you so about this one: a take on whether department stores are “really dead this time.” The article starts off by noting that since 2016, and with its latest announcement, Macy’s will have closed nearly half of its store base. The CEO noted that it was a case of “too many locations built for a different era.” And the article highlights three specific things that have gone wrong for department stores: too many bricks, too little listening (to customers), and too much that’s out of date. Basically, they missed big consumer shifts and got trapped into a case where it was just too much to overcome.
I think all three points are valid. Department stores were partly real estate businesses, and that has mostly been lost, which has eroded the value of brick & mortar locations. And when sales per square foot kept falling, there was a lot of blame on external factors instead of looking inward to see what customers were telling them they wanted. And without that voice to help guide them, department stores are also now missing the mark with products – missing that WFH has continued, for example.
This “different era” thing, though, is important. The three points are symptoms of a much deeper problem. A department store was an aggregator, a convenience factor of a one-stop-shop. It was built to drive customers to the store, where they would then pick from among the various choices presented there.
Consumers don’t shop that way any longer. They decide what they want to buy and then they decide where they want to buy it. In that situation, all brand value proposition, all basket-building for margin, is lost. And to fix it would’ve been far too radical. Who needs a Coach shop-in-shop when there’s a whole Coach store just a little ways into the mall? What value proposition can you offer a customer when all of the products they can get – and more – from your store are only a tab away on the browser and likeliy for a better price?
If anyone might have been able to pull off something truly transformational, it was Ron Johnson and what he was trying to accomplish at JCPenney. And he didn’t succeed. And while some department stores – even JCPenney – have found a way to survive, I don’t think any of them are truly thriving.
And in the Retail Winners camp, e.l.f. is building on Walmart’s investment in integrating commerce APIs into Roblox, by offering a real-world beauty kiosk inside Roblox. Consumers “aged 13 and up” can purchase a Roblox-exclusive limited-edition IRL product, and get a virtual item free. This is cool, and I’m definitely getting to where I may truly have to get into Roblox and Fortnight just to experience some of this stuff for myself (not enough to peer over my kids’ shoulders, sigh). But the most important part of this story is the “powered by Walmart’s APIs”.
Store Innovations
I couldn’t put Roblox/e.l.f. in the Store Innovations section, in general and also because I didn’t really see an in-store tie-in happening as part of the effort. But I do have two store innovations to share this week. First up is Petco and their Union Square NYC flagship. It’s worth clicking through to see the pictures of the place, it’s truly amazing. The store design looks like something out of Breakfast at Tiffany’s. It’s hardly recognizable as a pet store, even with all the dogs in the pictures. They put a lot of thoughtful design into making the store delightful to visit. The big question is, will that awe and wonder last several months later? Can the company keep the store fresh within the constraints of the design that looks so great today? This is the challenge with immersive experiences.
Next up is CAMP, the children’s toy / adventure store. The retailer is joining forces with RWS Global, “a provider of customized experiences across theatrical productions, events, and multimedia, to bolster immersive experiences. The first two big collaborations will focus on Disney’s Bluey x CAMP and Universal’s Trolls x CAMP. The new stores will have slime creation stations, a Splatter Room for painting, a “Campitheater” for live events and a party room.
A million years ago, I once worked for a little business unit loosely attached to Blockbuster called Viacom Retail Group. Its first stores were Nickelodeon stores. They looked like slime factories inside, with pressure valve wheels that had a degree of interactivity. It was way before its time in terms of immersive retail experiences, and ultimately killed off because it was way more profitable to just license the characters. We are getting closer to future where there are many fewer stores, but each store is like a Meow Wolf installation, a lot more theater, and a lot less (or more finely tuned) retail. I hope they’re building in some way to track all this, most especially to track the impact on loyalty and frequency of visits.
The Bottom Line
What did we learn about retail and tech strategy this week? One, it’s still highly uncertain out there, but if you’re not already thinking about how to regain share in the face of falling prices, you’re going to be way behind. Get reacquainted with promotions! Two, there’s still a lot of question about how much GenAI can do – and whether we’re building up too much hype for consumers. And three, yes, department stores are all but dead. But it’s not so important how it happened, as it is why it happened – and really digging back into root causes and not letting easy excuses stand. Finally, I had to blur the lines between retail innovation and store innovation. Which is great, actually. The two should be closer together than they are.

title: SAP BrandVoice: Here’s Why You Can Be Sure Your Starbucks Coffee Is 100% Sustainable
text:
The thing about innovation is that once we are past the “wow” moment, it quickly becomes mundane. If its practical implementation results in significant, long-lasting impact, that’s the proof that a new idea is meaningful.
This is often the case with how companies are using AI today, especially those that already have a long legacy of innovation, such as Salling Group, Denmark’s largest retailer.
A family affair
“People talk about AI as if it’s something very new, but we’ve been using it for many years, going through a long iterative process to reach its current, much more advanced format that has opened up new innovative cases we have not seen before,” said Alan Jensen, CIO of Salling Group. He was speaking at a session about empowering industries with AI at SAP Sapphire Barcelona hosted by Sven Denecken, SVP for SAP Industries and CX.
Jensen sees AI as just another tool in an evolutionary IT portfolio. The point of implementing more sophisticated systems is to help employees do their jobs better and facilitate engagement with customers, thereby improving customer experience. Most of the time with embedded AI, such as SAP’s new Joule copilot, employees are not even aware of the technology. They simply enjoy the benefits.
Jensen recounted the tale of young Herman Salling’s travels around the United States back in the 1950s. He was amazed to find markets where people could push a shopping cart around and pick the products off the shelves themselves. Not only that, but food and clothing were both available in the same store. He introduced the revolutionary concept of self-service markets in his home country Denmark with the supermarket chain Fotex, a name crafted from the words “food” and “textiles.”
Uncompromising commitment
Today the group’s brands include Starbucks, Netto, Føtex, Bilka, Salling and many others. Its wide range of products are sourced from all corners of the world. “As a group, we have a strong sustainability agenda, and we have a responsibility to ensure that our suppliers and their selected production sites comply with applicable laws, regulations, and employment rights,” said Jensen. “Salling Group is 100% owned by the Salling Foundations, and our purpose is really to give back to society.”
The most important step toward achieving its purpose is its uncompromising commitment to creating a net zero economy. To drive sustainable growth, the group has set ambitious, science- based targets to reduce emissions, in alignment with the terms of reference established by the Science Based Targets Initiative.
“It’s crucial to get our suppliers and partners on board by securing their total commitment as well,” said Jensen.
For example, using energy efficient technologies in a sustainable data center is of strategic importance to Salling. After discussions with SAP, the group announced a partnership with SAP and Microsoft to meet strict data center requirements in alignment with the science-based targets set for the company. This partnership will support Salling’s ambition to become CO2-neutral in its IT and digital operations by 2028.
“With this agreement, we will move our SAP platform to the RISE with SAP solution operated in Microsoft’s new Danish data center, on track to be one of the world’s most sustainable. I’m very happy to extend our successful partnership with SAP and look forward to taking the engagement to the next level,” said Jensen. “We’re challenging all our partners, not just SAP. For example, we’ve informed all our logistics partners they must be using fully electrified vehicles by 2028 if they want to continue transporting our goods.”
The role of AI
Like the commitment to sustainability, the nitty gritty aspects of AI have their own challenges, but they’re far outweighed by the benefits. In the supermarket landscape, defining the right sales prices when products reach end of use has become a major challenge. Jensen explained how AI is helping 60,000 employees make the right pricing decisions. With the new AI solution, products are now sold out on the exact expiration date, reducing food waste and delivering a higher margin.
“How we are using AI was an eye opener for our company and our top management,” said Jensen. “We are also using AI to predict how many people we need in the distribution center to fulfill the task for the day. During the morning, employees can see the speed of orders coming in and can determine what time they’ll be finished that day, at two, four, or six o'clock. They can then adapt inventory to make sure that we don't have more than necessary.”
Jensen’s team is now using AI on top of the very strong forecasting and replenishment tools from SAP, for example, to solve issues of cannibalization and to resolve product substitutions when items are sold out. “We’re building our AI capabilities to do it even better,” he said.
The other thing about innovation is that, once we are past the “wow” moment, it leads to even more opportunities for improvement – and that’s the real beauty of new ideas. As the Salling Group has demonstrated, it can bring people together to create a better world.
