title: Unpacking The GOP Two-Line Powerfully Packed Position Statement About Artificial Intelligence As Revealed In The Newly Released 2024 Republican Platform
text:
In today’s column, per reader urgings, I will go ahead and discuss the position statement recently released by the GOP about the present and future role of government regulation regarding Artificial Intelligence (AI). My approach will walk you through step-by-step what this is all about and share the larger context involved. In addition, I will mindfully parse the rather brief position statement, expand upon the points made, and give you a semblance of what it might further entail.
There are substantial societal, business, economic, and technological impacts at play.
It’s a big deal.
Buckle up for quite a ride.
As an aside, those of you interested in generally exploring matters surrounding the latest in AI and the ins and outs of the legal, governmental, policies, and political dynamics might find of interest my ongoing coverage as posted at the link here. Specific examples of especially noteworthy topics include my comprehensive look at how the law impacts advances in AI, see the link here, and how politics shapes the pace and direction of AI developments, see the link here. Many other of my postings do likewise.
My goal throughout is to provide a balanced perspective that highlights all views and doesn’t land on one side or the other. There are plenty of mainstream news media and social media diatribes that fail to see the world in anything other than one particular posture.
The desire here is to make sure that all sides of the coin get a fair and balanced airing.
Let’s do so.
Background Of Keen Relevance
Before I leap into the GOP statement, I believe it would be helpful to share with you a key AI consideration that arose during the current White House administration and is a (kind of) centerpiece of the GOP statement (not favorably, though, as you might imagine). Consider this to be essential background and context-setting material.
Hang in there, this will be worth it.
The matter has to do with an AI-oriented Executive Order that first happened in 2022, then another one in 2023, and they have both been carrying on ever since.
Turn back the clock and let’s take a time-travel glimpse at what occurred.
I previously examined that the White House published an Executive Order on October 4, 2022, known conversationally as an “AI Bill Of Rights” and I provided key insights at that time about the existing and future likely impacts of the stated approach on AI innovations, see my coverage at the link here. The analysis goes along with my ongoing examination of the latest in AI Ethics and AI Law on an enduring basis, see the link here.
Let’s do a quick review of the matter.
The White House indeed released on October 4, 2022, a white paper informally referred to as an “AI Bill of Rights” and which more officially was entitled “Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights: Making Automated Systems Work for the American People”. The document was the culmination of work by the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), a federal entity that was established in the mid-1970s and serves to advise the American President and the Executive Office on various technological, scientific, and engineering aspects of national importance.
The “AI Bill of Rights” depicts the asserted human rights that humankind ought to have with respect to the advent of AI in our daily lives. I emphasize this weighty point because some people were at first puzzled that maybe this was some kind of acknowledgment of AI having legal personhood and that this was a litany of rights for sentient AI and humanoid robots. You might make that interpretation since the title of the document refers to an “AI” bill of rights. I think you can see the potential confusion thereof.
Turns out that this is about human rights in an AI era. The idea is that this was a means of stipulating your rights as a human being when it comes to the advent of modern-day AI. Perhaps the document could have been entitled something like the “Human Bill Of Rights In Light Of AI” but that’s admittedly a mouthful.
Anyway, separately, if you are interested in or simply curious about the quietly fervent debate about whether AI ought to garner legal human rights, see my analysis at the link here.
In the White House “AI Bill of Rights”, there were five keystone categories:
- Safe and effective systems
- Algorithmic discrimination protections
- Data privacy
- Notice and explanation
- Human alternatives, consideration, and fallback
Much of the stipulations had to do with the litany of AI ethics precepts that were being popularly voiced at that time. For example, see my coverage of the United Nations call for ethical AI, see the link here, the Department of Defense (DoD) list of responsible AI precepts, see the link here, and even the Vatican’s indication of how AI ought to be ethically devised and fielded, see the link here.
The overarching viewpoint about this Executive Order was that it was relatively innocuous and smacked of mom and apple pie. There weren’t any teeth to it per se. More bark than bite, as they say.
At the time, I pointed out various criticisms that were being widely voiced:
- Nice try but not fully baked.
- Advisory only, not considered actual governmental policy.
- Not legally enforceable and altogether non-binding.
- Not comprehensive in comparison to other published works.
- Primarily broad concepts and absent of implementation details.
- Extremely difficult to turn into actual viable practical laws.
- Omits some key topics such as proposals for bans on AI.
- Lacks acknowledgment of the upsides of well-devised AI.
- Etc.
Let’s refer to that herein as AI Executive Order 2022.
This was the precursor to a more detailed and actionable Executive Order released on October 30, 2023, see my coverage and analysis at the link here.
I will refer to this newer one as the AI Executive Order 2023, which formally was entitled “Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence”. Many just referred to it as the “Trustworthy AI” pronouncement.
A plethora of controversy arose over this Executive Order due to definitions about what constitutes AI, requirements for reporting on the development of certain kinds of AI, prohibitions associated with ways in which AI might be devised or sold, stipulations about AI infrastructure and operators of such architecture, and so on. Less controversial, generally, were provisions tasking the federal government with figuring out what AI it is using, how AI is to be acquired and utilized in federal settings, safety procedures and precautions associated with federal AI usage, and the like.
Some provisions were generally liked or considered seemingly reasonable, while plenty of the provisions were disliked or at least hotly debated. An oft-heard comment was that sometimes you must take the bad (imperfect) to get the good. You can’t expect perfection. Perfection will never arrive. Accept what has been meted out and move on with your life.
Depending upon your perspective about the appropriate role of the government in overseeing or regulating AI, you might have loved the Executive Order or dearly hated it. Others were in the middle ground. This was especially possible because some of the more engaging portions were unlikely to kick into gear right away. It was conceivable that you could wait and see what transpires down the road, rather than putting up a big ruckus at that moment in time.
An added twist is worth noting.
In addition to the above, and this is an essential consideration, some vehemently argued that much of what was stated ought to be determined by lawmakers rather than the executive branch. If the provisions were truly needed and the public was at risk, certainly Congress would bring forth new AI laws to cover this. The use of an Executive Order was said to be an overreach.
Counterarguments were that Congress had seemingly become mired in numerous proposed AI bills and that it was unlikely that any new AI laws would get passed. Ergo, minimally as a stopgap, an Executive Order on AI was worthy and necessary. If Congress can’t get its act in order, the executive branch is duty-bound to fill in the missing pieces. That was a frequent exhortation.
This brings us up to current times.
I’ve been covering and tracking the numerous AI bills that have been floating around Congress and my readers well know that I’ve predicted nothing is going to substantively happen on those bills until we get past the November election. There isn’t enough momentum right now to bring urgent attention to new laws about AI. The only exception would be if a catastrophic nationwide AI incident occurred between now and the election, in which case there would be media and public outcry, which might be enough to drive Congress toward agreeing on something about a new AI law.
I don’t foresee any such AI calamity in that near-term timeframe that would be momentous enough to move the needle on this.
In recap, here’s where we are today:
- (i) AI Executive Order 2022 is said to be relatively innocuous.
- (ii) AI Executive Order 2023 is said to be relatively controversial.
- (iii) Congress is floating around lots of AI bills.
- (iv) Congress’ polarization is unlikely to pass any new AI laws near-term (mainly awaiting election results).
I believe this gets you up to speed sufficiently and I can then introduce the GOP statement in a manner that you are now familiar with the big picture into which the statement fits.
Thanks for your generous and appreciated patience.
GOP Platform For 2024 And Beyond
Our time travel did its job, and we are back in present day.
On Monday, July 8, 2024, a document entitled “2024 GOP Platform: Make America Great Again” was made available publicly by the GOP and had received approval by the platform committee of the Republican National Committee. The preamble is entitled “America First: A Return To Common Sense”. Overall, the document is considered a vision of the latest Republican platform across a wide swath of topics and will presumably be voted on for final ratification at the upcoming Republican National Convention.
Please note that the wording could end up being changed and thus realize that the wording as cited herein is based on the current draft and not necessarily the final say on the matter.
There are twenty chapters.
I won’t go over all of them, though it certainly is worthwhile to observe that to adequately understand any specific element within the document, doing so is best done by understanding the totality of what the document indicates. My advice is this. Take care in plucking out any line or two and falling into the classic trap of misrepresenting a claimed stated position that is potentially taken out of context.
I am endeavoring here to cover the AI position statement and proffer an overarching context as embedded within the document as a whole. The AI position statement is found in Chapter Three, and then within Item #5 of that third chapter.
Allow me to stepwise walk you to the AI position statement so you’ll have a semblance in your mind of where it is positioned in the overall document.
The third chapter, which contains the AI position statement, is entitled “Chapter Three: Build The Greatest Economy In History” and provides this opening summary overall regarding the intent of the third chapter:
- “Our Commitment: American Workers are the most productive, talented, and innovative on Earth. The only thing holding them back is the suffocating policies of the Democrat Party. Our America First Economic Agenda rests on five pillars: Slashing Regulations, cutting Taxes, securing Fair Trade Deals, ensuring Reliable and Abundant Low-Cost Energy, and championing Innovation. Together, we will restore Economic Prosperity and Opportunity for all Americans.”
I am sure you noted that the language is worded in what might be gently referred to as localized to particular tastes. It leaps off the page, as it were. This is seen as advocacy wording, naturally so, and would indubitably be found in similar opposing camp documents.
The third chapter has five main items.
Item number 5 in the third chapter is entitled “Champion Innovation” and makes this remark:
- “Republicans will pave the way for future Economic Greatness by leading the World in Emerging Industries.”
Within item number 5 there are three subcomponents: (a) “Crypto”, (b) “Artificial Intelligence”, and (c) “Expanding freedom, prosperity, and safety in space”.
The second subcomponent that is specifically on Artificial Intelligence, which is what we are laser-focused on here, says the following on a word-for-word cited basis (we finally got to this in my discussion here; your fortitude has once again been rewarded and much appreciated):
- “Artificial Intelligence (AI): We will repeal Joe Biden’s dangerous Executive Order that hinders AI Innovation, and imposes Radical Leftwing ideas on the development of this technology. In its place, Republicans support AI Development rooted in Free Speech and Human Flourishing.” (Source: 2024 GOP Platform, posted online July 8, 2024).
Observe that the AI-related statement consists of those two sentences.
Yes, just those two sentences.
I mention this because there has been a lot of media haranguing and consternation regarding the AI statement. Do realize that the kerfuffle is based on those two sentences. Of course, to a certain extent, the expressive language used in the statements perhaps fosters or spurs certain kinds of responses.
Two sentences can say a lot. It might not seem like much at a cursory glance especially if you aren’t “into” AI tech policy, but to be clear, the significance of those sentences has immense potential impacts.
We shall proceed to mindfully unpack the matter.
The Meaning Underlying The AI Position Statement
Sometimes, the way that something is worded can cause a reaction that might overlook or overshadow the essence of what is being said. I’m not suggesting that rabble-rousing wording should be ignored, and only suggesting that we can try to distill such wording to discover a core of what is being stated or implied.
Let’s try doing that.
My interpretation of the two-line AI-specific position statement is that the essence consists of these two keystones and their respective subordinated elements:
- (1) Repeal. The first step involves repealing the White House Executive Order, which I take to imply the AI Executive Order 2023 but could possibly also incorporate AI Executive Order 2022, just for completeness’s sake.
- (1a) Basis for repeal: Do so to curtail the various included seen-to-be hindrances to AI innovation.
- (1b) Another basis for repeal: Do so to untether various White House imposed constraints on the development of AI.
- (2) Replace. The second step consists of establishing and implementing a new replacement approach, which might be a new Executive Order, or perhaps anticipated congressional action, or both.
- (2a) Basis for the new approach: Aim to support AI development as rooted in free speech.
- (2b) Another basis for the new approach: Aim to support AI development as rooted in human flourishing.
The position statement then overall could be reimagined and reworded based on that outline, and might say something like this in a more measured tone:
- My reimagined draft — “Artificial Intelligence (AI): We intend to repeal the White House Executive Orders on AI and do so since we believe that the existing approach hinders AI innovation and imposes undue constraints on the development and advances in AI. In its place, we aim to devise and field policies that will actively support the development and advancement of AI, especially as rooted in vital principles entailing freedom of speech and human flourishing.”
I hope that sufficiently expresses the essence. Certainly, don’t want to inadvertently put words in anyone’s mouth and I trust that you realize I am only seeking to merely move us to a plain of existence that involves the keystones of the matters at hand.
Now that we have ascertained the crux of the matter, we can noodle a bit on it.
The Way Forward Is Calculable
I would assume that you are wondering about two major aspects at this juncture, consisting of what it is that might be repealed (we seem to know what this is), and what is it that will replace that which is intended to be repealed (we only have quite broad strokes suggested).
The first question about what is to be repealed seems rather clear, the stated intent is to repeal the White House Executive Orders on AI. Period, end of story. You can run with that answer. This would presumably involve striking out the stipulations on AI-related reporting requirements, AI evaluation approaches, AI uses and disuses limitations, and so on.
On paper, that’s straightforward.
Turns out life isn’t quite that simple.
There is a gaggle of policy provisions and proclamations that arise in the existing Executive Orders on AI, some of which already have been variously implemented. You might say that it is a recently planted tree that has already taken root.
Repealing it is somewhat muddled in that yes, you can proceed once in power to declare it null and void at a 30,000-foot level, assuming that legally this won’t be fought, which it probably would, but the lingering effects are a different beast. Trying to undo those already infused changes will be arduous since the tenacles have already been to some degree spread around.
Some pundits have already suggested that it won’t be feasible to truly repeal the already underway implementations due to implanted facets. Those could be deeply ingrained. Processes have at times been revamped to incorporate the provisions. People who are tasked with those processes are likely to be hesitant to give up those processes. Etc.
My thoughts are that this is pretty much the same switcheroo conundrum when any administration of one flavor is replaced by an administration of a different flavor. No matter which is in, and which is out, the same carping goes that undoing what was already done is going to be arduous. Sure, that’s par for the course.
To me, the idea of an impossibility in repealing the matter is not an especially viable argument to be made. The focus will be on how well-planned and performed is the repeal. If the repeal is simply a stroke of the pen, surely the repeal will be shallow and probably not make much of a day-to-day difference. Those seeking to undertake the repeal will need to realize that a whole bunch more will be needed to ensure an effective repeal, assuming that’s the desired goal.
All in all, a repeal seems viable and can be carried out if done with sensible and suitable forethought and determination.
The expectation would be that grand resistance will be afoot. There will be internal resistance by those already affixed to the provisions that have been implemented. There will be opposing political forces that will undoubtedly proclaim that the loss of those provisions is a surefire doom-and-gloom for human rights. The media will certainly chime in too.
Change is rarely easy.
The Lopsided Exhortations
One aspect that has already been voiced is the instant response world that we live in consists of foul cries about the repealing part of things — but doing so without also giving due consideration to the replacement part of things.
Allow me a moment to explain.
Suppose that someone tells you they are going to repeal your car, well, let’s say take away your car. If that’s all that you react to, there is little doubt that you would scream and holler. How are you going to get anywhere without your car? It is outrageous that you won’t have your car.
But suppose further that before veering into a knee-jerk reaction, the same indication about the repeal of the car is accompanied immediately by an indication that you will be getting a different car as a replacement. I assume that rather than being solely preoccupied with the repeal of your car, you are now seeking to find out what the replacement car consists of.
My gist is this.
Those assorted pundits that are decrying the repeal, ought to also be giving due consideration to the replacement. If their outcry is based only on the repeal, the other half of the equation is being neglected, either for calculated purposes or by rather myopic oversight.
That being said, for those who can see that there is a repeal plus an accompanying replacement, I certainly sympathize that we don’t know much about the envisioned replacement. There are vagaries of course that the replacement will consist of something about AI policies that will encompass freedom of speech and human flourishing.
Into this vacuum comes all manner of conjecture.
Some wildly predict that we will have no-holds-barred AI. All AI makers and those that field AI will have a heyday. Anything goes. This might spur the feared AI existential risk, namely that AI will spring into sentience or become Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and we didn’t see it coming. Why? Because whatever replacement policies are ultimately established, if any, let it happen.
